item.title: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry
item.abstract:
Note: We're running a new Minecraft colony with 25 GPT-6.1 Terra agents. Follow on Twitch Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice). We teamed up with Olam Labs , which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry. Minecraft Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's video pretraining work to Google DeepMind's agents defeating the Ender Dragon . We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game. github.com/yc-software/minecraft-agent-harness Civ50 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs. The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages. At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access. plans/settlement.md Download Settlement coordination (Ada)

item.title: A tiny world model running games on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W
item.abstract:
Using 2 small neural networks to generate and play the game at the same time on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W. The first one creates the game: given the current frame and the action, it predicts the next frame and the reward. The second one plays that game: it uses the generated frame and picks an action. Every frame above was sampled by the world model network, and the actions were taken by the actor network. Why I got interested in looped transformers, where one transformer block is applied several times with the same weights instead of stacking different layers. Reusing weights is cheap on memory, so I wanted to see if a looped world model could be small enough to run on a microcontroller. I picked the Pico 2 W because it is cheap and has an FPU, and small games because I could write the real versions directly into numpy and check every generated frame against them. Later I added a streaming RL agent so the board could also learn to play inside its own dream. Contents: the two networks · the games · the world model · the agents · quantization · on the chip · flashing · browser · reproduce · code layout The world model and the actor network 1: the world model network 2: the actor job frame + action → next frame + reward frame → action architecture looped transformer, q int8 MLP with two hidden layers, float32 size 26k–131k parameters 9k–16k parameters cost per frame 2–8M multiply-adds 9k–16k multiply-adds trained on recorded real games ( how ) with stream-x, in the real game or inside the dream ( how ) The size depends on the game, some games require more parameters to learn them to be playable, we tried to get to keep the number of the parameters small enough. On the chip neither network ever uses the real game: the actor only sees frames the world model, and the world model only gets actions from the actor. Both run on core 1 of the RP2350, while core 0 handles USB and the display. The pretrained actor can be swapped for a fresh stream-x agent that learns from scratch on the board. And any button press hands control to you, so you can play the dream yourself. The games Each game is a few hundred lines of numpy in src/tinyworldformer/games/ . It renders to a small grid of token ids, and one frame always holds the whole game state, so hidden state has to be drawn into the frame: the ball's heading is part of its token, and Doom-lite has a minimap. game frame rules random event world model exact frames, 2 loops Breakout 20×16 paddle, ball, 56 bricks, 5 lives the serve after a miss 26k params, 4.3M MACs 99.99% Doom-lite 32×32 raycast first-person view of an 8×8 maze; an enemy walks shortest paths to you; you shoot the enemy's respawn 55k params, 4.2M MACs 83.6% (see below) Flappy Bird 24×24 gravity, flaps, scrolling pipes the next gap height 46k params, 2.0M MACs 100% Pong 20×32 you against a CPU paddle that reacts late, first to 5 the serve after a point 46k params, 2.3M MACs 99.45% Pac-Man lite 48×48 23×21 maze, 249 pellets, two ghosts on shortest paths, 3 lives the ghosts' respawn 131k params, 8.2M MACs 86.4% "Exact frames" is the share of held-out transitions where every cell of the predicted frame matches the real game. Frames right after a random event are left out, since those can only be sampled, not predicted. Doom-lite's 3D view has 768 cells and a single shaded wall pixel off counts the whole frame as wrong, so its number looks worse than it plays; the game state is almost always right (see checking the dream ). You can play the real games in a terminal: uv run python -m tinyworldformer.games.play --game pacman (or breakout , doomlite , flappy , pong ). How the world model works Frames split into tokens The frame is cut into square patches: 2×2 cells in Breakout, 4×4 in Doom-lite, Flappy Bird and Pong, 6×6 in Pac-Man. That gives 36 to 80 tokens per game. A patch's embedding is the sum of one learned vector per cell, with a separate table for each position inside the patch so the cell order isn't lost. Every token also gets a position vector and the action's vector. Looped Transformer The model is a single transformer block (attention plus a ReLU MLP) with one set of weights, applied 1 to 4 times, with the input added back before every pass. The output after every pass is trained against the next frame, so at run time the loop count trades speed for accuracy. On the Pico to keep a decent frame rate we use uses two loops. The animation shows one held-out Doom-lite step. After one pass the model draws an enemy that isn't there, and each further pass removes part of it: 92, 35, 12, then 0 wrong cells. The bars on the right are the share of held-out frames each loop count gets exactly right. Here is a dreamed Doom-lite step decoded after 1, 2, 3 and 4 loops, with red boxes on cells that differ from the real rules: Exact held-out frames by loop count: loops Breakout Doom-lite Flappy Bird Pong Pac-Man 1 99.68% 59.8% 99.99% 98.47% 79.6% 2 99.99% 83.6% 100% 99.45% 86.4% 3 100% 85.9% 100% 99.60% 85.7% 4 99.96% 84.7% 100% 99.53% 84.4% Decoding The model outputs a score for every cell and every token. Turning those scores into a frame turned out to matter almost as much as the model, and it ended up as three rules (shown above on Pong): Background cells (walls, bricks, pellets, floor) each take their most likely token independently. Singletons (the ball, the player, each ghost) are placed with one choice over all (cell, token) pairs, so there is always exactly one of each. After a random event the choice is sampled among candidates within 2.2 logits of the best, so the world model samples a new serve or respawn instead of averaging them. Pac-Man and the ghosts are 2×2 sprites, but only one cell of each carries state (the mouth holds the heading; the ghost's lower-left cell holds whether a pellet is underneath). The other three cells are stamped from it instead of predicted. We implemented Rule 2 because the first Breakout model drew two balls at once; one global choice took exact frames from 91.6% to 99.7%. Checking the world model Accuracy on recorded data wasn't enough. An agent drives the dream into states the data never had, and any mistake there is something it can exploit. So the main check runs while an agent plays: read the game state back off the dreamed frame ( games/<game>.py: read ), apply the real rules to that state and the agent's action, and compare the result with the next dreamed frame and reward. 5,000 dreamed steps per game at 2 loops, with the shipped agent ( training/evalwm.py --agent ): game wrong game states wrong rewards wrong cells per step Breakout not read back; 0 frames with impossible tokens 6 (paid without a brick breaking) – Doom-lite 1 0 1.50 Flappy Bird 0 0 0.00 Pong 1 0 0.00 Pac-Man 742 38 0.39 Training First, agents play the real game and every step is recorded as one example (frame, action, next frame, reward), 1–3 million per game. Some episodes start from unusual states, like bricks with holes or random positions, so the data covers more of the game. Then the world model learns to predict the next frame with a per-cell cross-entropy loss: 30k steps, with the first 3–4k steps run in float, then int8 rounding switches on ( QAT ). The int8 weights are written into Rust source with every float stored as its exact bits. We check them with cargo test to reproduces the Python integer spec bit for bit, and then the firmware runs on the Pico. An agent trained in the world model reaches states the recorded data never had, so record real games with that agent and fine-tune the world model on everything. The agent in different games stated exploiting them so those are some fixes to it: Weighting the loss by "this cell changed" biased the model toward predicting change, so it drew two balls and broke two bricks. Weighting by where things can happen in the input frame, plus the global singleton choice, fixed it.

item.title: Samaya AI Releases Sterling: A 3B-Active Finance Research Agent Model that Beats Claude Fable 5.1 on FrontierFinance at 11x Lower Cost
item.abstract: Samaya AI has released Samaya Sterling , a post-trained model for agentic financial research. Sterling is built on NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning , a 30B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. On Samaya’s FrontierFinance benchmark , it scores 58.9%. Claude Fable 5.1 scores 55.9%. Each Sterling question costs $0.61, against $6.89 for Fable 5.1. For developers, the takeaway is a concrete recipe: co-train a small model with its harness, and it can win in a narrow domain. Samaya Sterling is a LoRA post-trained version of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, tuned to work as a financial research agent. It plans research, calls finance tools, gathers evidence and hands findings to a separate report writer. According to Maithra Raghu’s X announcement , it started as a 2-person effort on agentic orchestration efficiency. Samaya team adapted its production finance harness for a small model. Detailed guidance was stripped from the system prompt and tool descriptions. Tools were merged to shorten the prompt. Two helper models manage context. A condenser shortens long tool results. A compactor summarizes the trace as it grows. A research budget caps how long the agent works. After that, the report writer answers from what was found. Training used LoRA on Tinker , Thinking Machines Lab’s training API. It ran in 4 stages: FrontierFinance has 220 public queries scored against expert-written rubrics. The grader uses a 3-model judge panel. Samaya team states that no benchmark question was used in training. Checkpoints were chosen on 100 internal validation questions. Sterling scores 58.9% at $0.61 and 282 s per question. Fable 5.1 scores 55.9% at $6.89 and 268 s. Samaya’s own high-effort system scores 2.9 points lower at $1.81. Every stage added quality: 42.5% (base), 51.4%, 54.8%, 57.5%, then 58.9%. Median tool calls rose from 3 to 17. In high-effort mode, Sterling reaches 60.6% at $1.83 and 372 s. On the hardest third, it rose from 31.8% to 45.2%. The model itself costs $0.04 per question. Tools and helper models make up the rest of the $0.61. FrontierFinance figures for all columns come from the Samaya blog and are self-reported. Check out the technical blog , the FrontierFinance benchmark , the dataset and the grader repo . item.title: Meet TokenEconomizer: Microsoft’s Plugin That Cuts Coding Agent Costs by Up to 30.9%
item.abstract: A team of researchers from Microsoft Research and UC Berkeley have released TokenEconomizer , an open-source cost controller for coding agents. TokenEconomizer is a plugin that learns from past sessions in a repository to cut waste in later ones. It works with Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI and Pi. It does not touch model weights or agent code. On 277 SWE-Bench tasks, it lowered mean cost by 18.4% to 30.9% across 5 agent-model settings. Every agent turn re-bills the system prompt, every loaded tool schema and the full history. The research team profiled 60 SWE-Bench tasks across 6 repositories using Claude Code with Opus 4.8. They found 3 recurring sources of waste: They also tested 3 fixed open-source strategies: RTK , Serena and Aider’s RepoMap . None was cheaper everywhere. All 3 cut cost on Django and raised it on SymPy. TokenEconomizer is an external controller that treats the agent as a black box. It keeps a state per repository, built from completed traces. Before each task, it sets 3 policies through the prompt, the tool settings and the event stream. An LLM proposer turns trace digests into 1-line facts, such as the working test command. Each fact carries regex detectors that check later traces without a model call. A fact enters the prompt after 3 confirmations on tasks with non-overlapping edited files. Its need rate must also stay at or above 0.4. One contradiction counts as 5 confirmations, so wrong facts retire quickly. Shell, read, write and edit tools are always kept. Other tools are masked after 3 consecutive unused tasks, or when an LLM judge marks them irrelevant. The full catalog returns every 5 tasks for a re-audit. On Django with Claude Code, the first request on task 2 fell from 43,351 to 16,295 prompt tokens. The controller learns a turn budget: 1.25 times the 90th percentile of successful run lengths. Cheap rule checks flag repeated failures or dense errors. An LLM judge then decides if the agent is stuck, at 0.7 confidence or higher. A stuck agent gets 1 redirect, then a stop if the loop recurs. Source: arXiv 2610.22732 , Table 1. Costs include all controller calls. 3 seeds per setting. Pass@1 improved in 4 of 5 settings. Lower reasoning effort saved cost but cut Pass@1 by 1.8 to 10.3 points. RTK alone raised cost in 12 of 30 repository-setting cells, and RepoMap in 15. Savings build over time. Most repositories cost more at first, but all were cheaper by the sixth task. Alone on Claude Code, tool pruning saved 13.2% to 17.7%, micro-skills 11.8% to 14.3%, and the loop guard 5.4% to 7.1%. Results also held outside SWE-Bench. Costs fell 16.0% to 21.2% on Web-Bench and 16.5% to 19.6% on CredData. ReposVul saw only 6.4% to 9.3%, because shorter runs leave less to remove. Cost rows: TokenEconomizer paper. Licenses and claims: each project’s repository or docs. The plugin needs one of the 4 agents and Python 3.10 or newer. On Claude Code, clone the repo, add it as a marketplace, then run claude plugin install tokeneconomizer@tokeneconomizer . Learned data stays local in ~/.tokeneconomizer . Tool pruning and the loop guard are on by default. Micro-skills are off by default, because the proposer adds model calls. Check out the Paper , GitHub Repo and Project Page . item.title: AI Security Agents Compared: Claude, Codex, Mantis, Cloudflare
item.abstract: Anthropic, OpenAI, Cloudflare and Google now each ship an AI agent that hunts security bugs in source code. We checked the repos, docs and technical details behind each one. The key finding: all 4 tools converge on one design. One agent finds a bug, a separate agent tries to disprove it, and only survivors get a patch. The differences are in where they run, who can use them and how much proof they demand. The problem every one of them is solving is noise. Google’s security team writes that sloppy AI code scanning produces hallucinated bugs and true-positive rates under 7% . A scanner that is wrong 93% of the time costs reviewers more than it saves. The shared fix is separation of duties. The agent that reports a finding never gets to confirm it. Cloudflare states the rule directly in its README: the verifier is never the agent that found the bug. Anthropic, OpenAI and Google each describe a similar validation step before anything reaches a report. The second driver is offense. Anthropic team states that it built its scanner partly because attackers were already using AI models to find exploitable flaws, per The Hacker News . Google opens its Mantis post by noting that models can now discover and exploit bugs with little human help. What it is: A multi-agent vulnerability scanner that runs inside a Claude Code session. It is the local version of Anthropic’s hosted Claude Security product, per the plugin README . How it works: Agents map the architecture, build a threat model, hunt across every component and verify each finding independently. The plugin offers 3 jobs from one menu: scan the codebase, scan changes, or suggest patches, per Claude Code docs . Output: A Markdown report along with a SARIF 2.1.0 file for GitHub code scanning. Each finding carries severity, a CWE category, impact and reproduction steps. Patches are drafted in a scratch copy and land as F<n>.patch files. The plugin never commits, pushes or opens a pull request on its own. Cost and access: It makes no model calls of its own, so there is no separate API key. Scans count against your Claude plan’s usage limits. Timeline: Anthropic opened a limited preview called Claude Code Security in February 2026. The hosted product reached public beta for Enterprise customers on Claude Opus 4.7 . The Claude Code plugin entered beta on July 22, 2026, per Cybersecurity News . In August, the hosted scanner moved to Claude Mythos 5, per Dataconomy . Where it fits: Anthropic positions it as one layer. The security-guidance plugin checks code as Claude writes it, and /security-review does a single pass on a branch. Claude Security is the on-demand deep scan. What it is: A CLI and TypeScript SDK, published as @openai/codex-security, for finding, validating and fixing vulnerabilities. How it works: It scans a whole repo, selected paths, or a Git diff. A –mode deep flag runs parallel discovery workers. It validates candidate findings, generates patches and can verify existing fixes. A cs policy command drafts a SECURITY.md that tells future scans what counts as a vulnerability in your project. Output: Threat models, SARIF, JSON or CSV exports, plus publishing to Linear. It can import GitHub code-scanning alerts and suggest owners from Git history. A GitHub Action runs scheduled or pull-request scans; findings are report-only by default. Cost and access: The client is Apache-2.0, but the scanner behind it is not. DevOps.com notes the CLI and SDK stay in limited beta for approved customers. The README lists OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, OpenRouter and Fireworks AI as providers. Requires Node.js 22.13+ and Python 3.10+. What it is: An MIT-licensed skill that turns any capable coding agent into a security auditor. How it works: A 6-phase audit: Requirements: A coding agent that supports tool use and parallel sub-agents, plus Node.js for the validators. It also wants an OS-enforced sandbox with no external network. Without one, leads stay needs_validation instead of being executed. npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill –skill security-audit Then ask the agent: “security audit this codebase.” Output defaults to ~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N>, outside your repo. The data behind it: Cloudflare published the skill on June 18, 2026, with its post Build your own vulnerability harness . The roughly 450-line skill seeded an internal harness that now scans 128 repos. Cloudflare reports these lifetime numbers: Better recon context cut the first-pass rejection rate from 40% to 11%. Cloudflare also uses one model for discovery and a different model for triage, so models check each other. What it is: An Apache-2.0 set of security-review skills plus an ADK reference harness for AI coding agents. Google team states that it is part of how it finds and fixes bugs internally. How it works: Mantis reads the repo’s history to learn from past security fixes. It builds a hierarchical summary tree, condensing files into directory and root summaries. Google team states that this cut token overhead by over 85% . It then generates a threat model and hypotheses, hunts, deduplicates and critiques findings. What sets it apart: Reproduction and patch verification. Mantis tries to reproduce each bug, from a static exploit sketch up to a unit test or mock server. It patches with an adversarial loop that attacks the fix. It also calibrates severity against a rubric to stop “thousands of criticals.” A mantis-advise skill then feeds what it learned back into code generation. Setup: Clone the repo and point any coding agent at it, or run the ADK harness directly. The harness supports a –focus prompt such as “look for IDOR” and a –max-tokens spend ceiling. At least 12 more agent-based vulnerability tools shipped or went public in 2026. Almost all repeat the same find-then-independently-verify loop. They split into free harnesses you run yourself and commercial or internal platforms. AppSec Santa also tracks harnesses from Anthropic (defending-code-reference-harness), Trail of Bits, Capital One (vulnhunter) and Cisco (ai-deep-sast). Cisco’s runs fully local on Foundation-Sec-8B, so no code leaves the machine. The pattern holds across vendors: deterministic engines or validators do the proving, models do the reasoning, and a human approves every fix. Cloudflare’s own architecture suggests a practical combination. Run discovery with one tool or model, then validate with a different one. Different models surface different shares of the bugs. item.abstract: 輝達團隊基於 MiniMax H3 開源影片增強方案，最高支援 4K 重生成 量子位的朋友們 2026-10-30 15:31:11 來源： 量子位 輝達與麻省理工學院團隊，在 Hugging Face 釋出了影片增強專案 Open-H3-Regenerate-2K 的模型權重 近日，由輝達與麻省理工學院研究人員組成的 Efficient-Large-Model 團隊，在 Hugging Face 釋出影片增強專案 Open-H3-Regenerate-2K 的模型權重，配套推理程式碼已在 NVlabs/Sana 倉庫開放。該方案基於 MiniMax H3，將低解析度影片草稿重新生成為高解析度影片，支援 2560×1440 的 2K 輸出，最高可實現 3840×2160 的原生 4K 重生成。 MiniMax H3 的完整系統包含多模態上下文處理、基礎音影片生成和高解析度重生成等環節。其中，已開放權重的 H3-Base 負責生成 768P 音影片，官方 H3-Regenerate-2K 模組通過 API 提供服務。此次釋出的專案複用 H3 基礎模型的生成能力，為高解析度重生成環節提供了一套可自行部署的開放實現。 在細化模型的訓練階段，研究團隊保持 H3 Transformer 主幹與影片 VAE 的原有參數不變，僅訓練新增的細化 LoRA。推理時，細化 LoRA 與 LightX2V FL2VA Turbo、LMS Sharp 等社群介面卡合併使用，通過三步去噪，在目標解析度下重新生成畫面細節。影片草稿中的場景、佈局和運動資訊，則為這一過程提供基礎。 為提高推理效率，專案採用社群開發的潛空間放大器，直接放大影片的潛在表示，減少高解析度下重複解碼、編碼的開銷。同時，方案結合 SoL-Engine 的稀疏注意力、低精度計算和快速 VAE 解碼器，對細化與解碼環節進行加速。 專案團隊公佈的測試顯示，在單張 NVIDIA B200 GPU、預熱後的測試條件下，一段約 5 秒影片的潛空間放大、三步細化和 2K 解碼合計耗時，由未最佳化實現的 87.26 秒降至 22.45 秒，處理速度約為原來的 3.9 倍。其中，快速解碼器將影片解碼耗時從約 15 秒降至約 1.6 秒。 畫質方面，專案團隊在 RefinerBench-150 上進行了對比評測。在相同輸入、相同 2K 輸出條件下，Open-H3-Regenerate-2K 在感知質量評測 UniPercept 上的平均分為 60.0，官方 H3-Regenerate-2K API 為 53.4。VBench 評測中，該方案的美學質量、成像質量和主體一致性得分更高，官方 API 在運動平滑度和動態程度上仍略優。 MiniMax H3 在今年 8 月開放權重，圍繞 H3 展開的微調、蒸餾和工具適配迅速增多，吸引了海內外研究團隊與社群開發者參與，一個月內下載量超過 2400 萬次，產生超過 300 個公開衍生模型，H3 成為 2026 年全球下載量最高的模型之一。 其中，輝達與 MIT 聯合圍繞 H3 的開發覆蓋了不同方向。除本次影片增強方案外，該團隊還發布了基於 H3 Ref2VA 構建的流式影片渲染模型 StreamRender-H3，以及從 H3 影片 VAE 蒸餾而來的快速解碼器 Sol-H3-VAE，分別面向互動式影片渲染和解碼效率最佳化。 此前，LightX2V 推出的 MiniMax-H3 Turbo 提供四步、八步等蒸餾版本，社群微調模型 Singularity 則著重最佳化動作表現、面部細節與視覺風格。海外團隊 FastVideo、Pika 也分別釋出了 FastH3 四步預覽版本和六步取樣的 Pika H3 Flex；ComfyUI、Unsloth 則通過適配權重和量化版本，將 H3 帶入更多本地創作工作流。 本文由MiniMax提供，量子位獲授權轉載，觀點歸原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 MiniMax 量子位的朋友們 好萊塢最缺的答案，被這家 10 億美元估值的 AI 影視獨角獸寫進了片單 2026-10-30 從學習人類到學習機器人同伴，清華大學聯合無問芯穹、智元提出具身智慧規模化落地新路徑 2026-10-30 前排圍觀！MEET2027報名通道正式開啟，首批重磅嘉賓已就位 2026-10-30 文遠知行001號員工帶隊，景爍科技首輪融資數千萬美元 2026-10-29 相關閱讀

item.title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
authors: Somya Chatterjee, Harshita Sahijwani, Min Chen, Sushmitha Rajeswari Muppa, Dayquan Julienne, Irene Shaffer, Chandra Inguva, Jenny Chen, Minha Hwang, Sam Ade Jacobs
item.abstract: Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars: Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ? In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve. Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful. To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources. Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure. We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage: This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes. While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in. We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios. Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions: While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including: This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results. Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline . Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk. Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline. This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible. Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions. On synthetic data quality , our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments. On scale and efficiency , each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals.

item.title: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock
item.abstract: Worldwide Express (part of ShipStation Global) had built something big: approximately $5 billion in systemwide revenue, over 75 less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers. But that same scale had a hidden cost. Every month, $15 million in free cash flow sat frozen, locked in billing exceptions no one had resolved yet. Each one had to be chased down by hand, carrier by carrier, with its own rules to check. Worldwide Express outsourced to a team that worked cases one at a time, calling customers and carriers for each dispute. The exceptions piled up, cash stayed stuck, and every order took longer to turn into money. Worldwide Express worked with AWS and LTM to build a multi-agentic AI solution with Amazon Bedrock that plugs directly into their transportation management system (TMS), SpeedShip. Six months after launch, the company reported a 75 percent reduction in active exceptions, a 4-week improvement in time-to-cash, $1M annual savings, and a one-time $10M free cash flow infusion. In this post, we describe the challenge, explain how Worldwide Express designed the multi-agent solution, and share the results. In LTL freight, roughly 14 percent of invoices fail the standard three-way match between the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the carrier invoice. When a match fails, the invoice enters exception handling. For Worldwide Express, exceptions fell into three categories: Each exception triggered a five-step manual process: With each carrier operating under its own tariff structure and dispute workflow, this process consumed most of the FinOps team’s bandwidth. Rule-based process automation (RPA) can handle structured, predictable workflows. However, exception resolution requires contextual judgment: interpreting a carrier’s accessorial policy, comparing charges against shipment data, and deciding validity given a carrier, exception type, and dollar amount. That variability is what made the problem a fit for the agentic AI framework. In June 2025, Worldwide Express engaged the AWS Business Transformation & Value Advisory team to identify 19 automation opportunities across the Order-to-Cash lifecycle. Knowing the business value of exceptions automation, Worldwide Express moved from assessment to production in less than 6 months. The solution runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock provides AI reasoning, and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is the engine. The design calls for fine-grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed between agents. Building the framework directly on Amazon EC2, with Amazon Bedrock providing inference, keeps that orchestration logic fully in the team’s hands and supports open source agent libraries. Production controls of business logic make each agent’s role, inputs, and decision boundaries explicit and auditable. In a billing-dispute workflow, every automated decision needs to be explainable. When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents, each handling a specific type of billing dispute: Each agent pulls specific carrier billing rules and policies before making a recommendation. After the exception is resolved, the system generates a plain-language note explaining what was found and what action was taken. Each custom agent has an instruction prompt (defining its role, decision boundaries, and output format), a set of actions (integrations into SpeedShip), and access to carrier-specific knowledge bases. By using Amazon Bedrock, each agent accesses a suitable foundation model through a single API while inheriting existing AWS governance. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . The agents connect to SpeedShip through the same APIs that analysts use. That means the AI sees exactly what a human reviewer would see (contract rates, shipment details, delivery proof) and writes its resolution into the same workflow. SpeedShip has APIs on AWS, so the agents wire into the same endpoints as other existing systems. Every carrier has different billing rules, fee definitions, and dispute procedures. Worldwide Express stores each carrier’s documentation: tariff rules, surcharge definitions, dispute steps, and variance thresholds. When an agent processes an exception, it retrieves that specific carrier’s policies and standard operating procedure (SOP) documents before deciding, so each decision is grounded in the carrier’s own rules. The same three agents handle all carriers without any carrier-specific code. The approval step was necessary for FinOps adoption during the initial rollout. Initially, a human reviewer would use the existing SpeedShip UI to approve recommendations before they’re finalized. Eventually when accuracy exceeded 99 percent, bulk approval became the default. Worldwide Express’s team built dashboards tracking automation rate by carrier, error rate by exception type, resolution time, and human override frequency. When a reviewer rejects a recommendation, the system logs the feedback. The team refines instruction prompts and knowledge bases based on rejection history, steadily increasing automation coverage. The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow, from exception detection through the three specialized agents to human approval. In the diagram, exceptions from the data sources (the SpeedShip TMS, a shipping system, an electronic data interchange (EDI) server, and carrier and vendor portals) are detected and routed to one of three agents. Each agent runs on Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling, uses an agent framework with its own prompt, tools, and carrier knowledge base, and calls Amazon Bedrock for model inference. The agents produce a resolution report. Cost finalization and an AI-written note then go to a human reviewer for approval in the SpeedShip analyst UI. Figure 1: Worldwide Express’s AI-powered exception handling architecture on AWS Six months in, Worldwide Express has deployed the solution across over 40 LTL carriers. The agents currently close 10,000 (approximately 50 percent) exceptions weekly with a less than 1 percent error rate. This shifted the FinOps team’s time from routine resolution to complex, high-value disputes. The impact shows up most clearly in the backlog of active exceptions, which fell from $15M in June 2025 to $4M six months later, a 75 percent reduction. Worldwide Express unlocked $10M in freed-up cash flow, over $1M in annual cost savings, and 60x first-year ROI. The company reports time-to-cash improving by four weeks. “With AWS, we’ve automated more than 40 percent of weekly billing exceptions, significantly reducing costs and accelerating billing cycles from days to minutes. Today, we release approximately $10 million more in customer billings each week at a speed that simply wasn’t possible before.” — Nathanael Pearson, VP of FinOps, Worldwide Express Worldwide Express is already expanding this approach to other parts of the Order-to-Cash cycle. For logistics companies managing high carrier volumes, the path forward is to start small. Automate the most repetitive exception type first, prove accuracy, then scale across the rest of the portfolio. Worldwide Express’s exception automation shows what’s possible when agentic AI meets a well-scoped business problem. The combination of Amazon Bedrock, carrier-specific knowledge bases, and a human-in-the-loop approval design let Worldwide Express move from assessment to production in less than 6 months while maintaining financial controls. The company is now expanding automation to other Order-to-Cash processes. To explore whether a similar approach might work for your organization, request a conversation with your account team or learn more about Amazon Bedrock . item.title: Build Specialized Agents on a Stack You Control with NVIDIA NemoClaw
item.abstract: Building an autonomous agent requires a model, a harness, and domain-specific tools. To deploy an agent more securely, developers need a runtime that enforces policies, along with optimization and observability tools for reliable execution. For production agents, the challenge lies in making these agents capable and safe to operate with access to real enterprise systems and data. This post explains how these components work together, with a focus on how NVIDIA NemoClaw open blueprints enable developers to build specialized agents on a stack they can own, customize, and run. This post provides criteria to help developers integrate NemoClaw with a harness they already use: OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, or LangChain Deep Agents. What an agent harness provides An agent requires four things: A model that reasons . A harness that defines how the agent operates. Tools and skills that extend its capabilities. A runtime that governs what the agent can access and do in production. NemoClaw works with agent harnesses NemoClaw open blueprints currently support three harnesses: OpenClaw can access files and applications, write code, spawn sub-agents, and maintain context across sessions. It runs on your own machine or server and supports long-running sessions, memory, and scheduled tasks. Hermes Agent , from Nous Research, is designed to get better with use. As teams correct the agents’ approach and repeat workflows, Hermes captures those patterns as durable skills that can be reused in future work. LangChain Deep Agents provides a customizable harness for complex, multistep tasks. It combines planning, file-based context management, memory, and delegation to specialized subagents. Each harness gives an agent skills, tools, orchestration, and memory. Using NemoClaw for full-stack production agents NemoClaw is not a competing harness, and it is not a runtime. It is a collection of blueprints that assembles an open agent stack on top of the harness selected by the developer. The stack combines model and harness optimization with runtime governance. Each NemoClaw blueprint brings together four components: A tuned open harness, such as Hermes Agent, LangChain Deep Agents, or OpenClaw, optimized to work with NVIDIA Nemotron. Nemotron open models . NVIDIA NeMo tools for optimization, including NVIDIA NeMo Relay for observing and improving agent execution, plus routing capabilities that can help improve throughput, cost, and reliability. NVIDIA OpenShell is the secure runtime that governs agent access to files, networks, credentials, and tools. If you are already building with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, or LangChain Deep Agents, a NemoClaw blueprint can assemble the surrounding stack without requiring you to rewrite the agent. Figure 1. NemoClaw is an open blueprint that works with several agent harnesses Why co-optimizing the model and harness matters An agent combines a model and a harness. The model thinks, while the harness provides the environment in which it operates. When the two are matched, the model can focus on the task. When they aren’t, it may ask for context again, stop early, or loop without progress. For example, LangChain tuned its Deep Agents harness for Nemotron 3 Ultra by adjusting prompts, tools, and middleware without retraining the model. Starting from an already strong baseline, the harness tuning brought Nemotron 3 Ultra to near-frontier performance at approximately 10x lower cost per run compared with leading closed models. The NemoClaw blueprint for LangChain Deep Agents packages these optimizations directly. Every developer using LangChain Deep Agents with Nemotron 3 Ultra can access these optimizations without reproducing the tuning work. The tuned Nemotron 3 Ultra model profile is available through LangChain on GitHub . When to use each Use a harness such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, or LangChain Deep Agents to build and experiment with the agent’s skills, tools, memory, and orchestration logic. Use a NemoClaw blueprint to assemble and run a specialized agent on an open stack that combines a tuned harness, models, optimization, telemetry, and OpenShell runtime controls. Question Agent harness NemoClaw blueprint What it is Software that manages how an agent uses tools, maintains context, and carries out tasks A reference stack that combines a supported harness with models, optimization tools, and a runtime What it provides Tools, skills, memory, and orchestration A tuned harness, models, optimization tools, and OpenShell runtime controls How they work together Provides the agent’s execution logic within the stack Combines the harness with the other stack components When to use it To build and customize an agent’s behavior To assemble and run an agent with model and harness optimization and runtime controls Table 1. Roles and capabilities of an agent harness and a NemoClaw blueprint A harness helps you build a capable agent. A NemoClaw blueprint helps you run that agent on an open stack with model and harness optimization, telemetry, and runtime governance. Example: A memory-driven Chief of Staff, built on Hermes The NemoClaw community repository includes a memory-driven Chief of Staff recipe. The agent maintains a persistent, human-readable model of the people, projects, priorities, and working patterns it encounters, so it doesn’t have to reconstruct context from scratch on every task. It is built as a deployable Hermes profile for NemoClaw, as outlined in the technical design walkthrough. The recipe shows the stack working together rather than in isolation. OpenShell governs the agent’s file system, process, and network access, and keeps credentials for managed inference and Model Context Protocol (MCP) connections outside the sandbox. This helps keep the agent bound by policy even when its memory or retrieved context leads it toward an unintended action. NeMo Relay is integrated natively into the Hermes session. It closes trace spans at real session boundaries, including a new session, reset, or expiry, and exports the resulting trajectories for audit and further optimization. Importance of agent governance Every NemoClaw reference includes OpenShell, the runtime that adds security and policy enforcement around the agent harness and tools, governing the actions a model can take. The OpenShell tutorial covers how to create your first policy to prevent data exfiltration to GitHub. NemoClaw references include more sophisticated OpenShell policies that govern agent connections across many different internal tools, sites, and communication channels. Deploy across cloud, data center, and local systems NemoClaw agents can run in the cloud, in data centers, on NVIDIA DGX Spark, and on NVIDIA RTX PCs and workstations. A NemoClaw clinical agent for a hospital and a NemoClaw simulation agent for electronic design automation can run on the same stack while using entirely different tools and skills. NemoClaw agents can also work alongside frontier agents. Claude, Codex, or Cursor agents can delegate domain-specific subtasks to NemoClaw-powered specialists running on open models and owned infrastructure. item.title: Baseten Releases joey-1, a 2B Decision Model at $0.01 per 1M Tokens
item.abstract: Baseten has released joey-1 , a 2B model from its in-house research lab, Base Labs. The joey-1 decision model returns a label and a calibrated probability instead of generated text. It targets high-volume routing, classification and guardrail checks. Baseten prices it at $0.01 per million input tokens , with open weights on Hugging Face under MIT. joey-1 is a 2B decision model from Baseten’s Base Labs that answers typed questions in 1 forward pass. You send a state (text or images) and 1 or more questions. The model returns a probability for every option of every question. It does not write free-form text that your application must parse. joey-1 is the third member of a family. Baseten shipped mammoth-1 (27B) and elephant-1 (9B) last week. All 3 share training data and the /v1/systemone API, so switching is a 1-line change. Base Labs post-trained Qwen3.5-2B with a full fine-tune of the language model. The vision encoder stays frozen. Full-attention layers use a block-bidirectional mask. All questions are answered from 1 shared-prefix prefill, so extra questions add little cost. Training details from the model card : Calibration lets you set a confidence threshold. Uncertain answers can escalate to elephant-1, mammoth-1 or a human. Baseten reports a P50 end-to-end latency of 20 ms for an average 2,000-token request. That is about 2.5x faster than elephant-1 (49 ms). The blog’s TL;DR also claims 5x faster than comparable decision models, without naming them. Model APIs charge $0.01 per 1M input tokens; output and cached input are listed at $0.00. elephant-1 costs $0.035 and mammoth-1 costs $0.10. Baseten’s example: 10M support tickets a month at about 500 tokens each is 5B tokens. That is about $50 on joey-1, versus $500 on mammoth-1. All scores below are self-reported on Baseten’s model card . On the Jev Decision Index 0.4 public split, joey-1 scores 63.30. That ranks #37 of 230 models and is the top score under 4B. item.title: Edge0 Releases Audio8-TTS-Realistic, a 0.6B Voice Cloning TTS Model
item.abstract: Edge0 has released Audio8-TTS-Realistic , an open-weight text-to-speech model for zero-shot voice cloning. Audio8-TTS-Realistic is a 0.6B-parameter model that clones a voice from 1 reference clip and transcript. It supports 23 languages, 12 more than its predecessor. The weights and code ship under Apache 2.0 . For developers, the catch is competitive multilingual accuracy at a size that is cheap to fine-tune and serve. It is the second 0.6B release in Edge0’s Audio8 TTS family. It builds on Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b and keeps the same Transformers inference interface. The repository bundles the checkpoint, a 44.1 kHz neural audio codec, tokenizer, processor and custom code. It can also generate speech without a reference voice. New languages are Arabic, Finnish, Hindi, Indonesian, Malay, Norwegian, Portuguese, Russian, Swedish, Thai, Turkish and Vietnamese. The model uses a dual-autoregressive (DualAR) design inspired by Fish Audio S2 Pro . According to the technical research report , the slow branch is built on Qwen2.5 0.5B. It has 24 layers at width 896 and runs at about 21.5 frames per second. Each step predicts text tokens plus the first audio codebook. A shallow 4-layer fast branch then predicts the remaining 9 codebooks in parallel. Sequential compute therefore happens only at the frame level. The team argues that word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) miss rhythm, pauses and timing. A model can score well on both and still sound synthetic. The critic scores each output against a matched human recording of the same sentence. It was trained on a quality ladder built from 6 open-source TTS systems. These were ranked in a private blind listening study, with human recordings at the top. Synthetic pause compression adds finer rungs to the ladder. An identity-erasure loss stops the critic from rewarding generator fingerprints. The critic head has about 3M parameters on top of a frozen WavLM-large encoder. A duration penalty also kicks in beyond 1.35x the reference length. This blocks the policy from gaming the critic with slower speech. The final stage used only Chinese and English prompts. It still improved both aggregate metrics on the 13 lower-resource languages. Their error fell from 22.53% to 20.77%, and SIM rose from 0.637 to 0.679. All numbers below are self-reported error rates, where lower is better. On CV3, Audio8 beats VoxCPM2 (5.35%), CosyVoice3-1.5B (6.89%) and Qwen3-TTS-1.7B (7.73%). On MiniMax, Qwen3-TTS-1.7B scores 27.41%, but it officially supports only 10 of the 24 test languages. Larger models still lead elsewhere. Higgs TTS 3 reports 4.41% on CV3 and 2.74% on MiniMax. Qwen3-TTS-1.7B averages 1.01% on Seed-TTS. Edge0 itself calls its table a reference comparison, since evaluation pipelines and text normalization differ. VoxCPM2’s CV3 average is computed from its per-language table. Install PyTorch 2.5+ and Transformers 4.57+, then load with trust_remote_code=True . Voice cloning needs a clean reference clip and its exact transcript. The GitHub repo adds a CLI, batching and supervised fine-tuning scripts. For GPU serving, an SGLang Omni adapter provides paged attention, dynamic batching and an OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/speech API. Edge0 notes throughput and streaming were not benchmarked. A free Playground runs on Hugging Face ZeroGPU. Check out the Paper , Model Weights , Repo and Samples . item.title: Was I wrong about open models & cyber risks?
item.abstract: Last week coined the term “ Black October “ after an onslaught of critical vulnerability disclosures, including PHP2Shell and GitLab, signified the moment when the cyber risks of AI models started to materialize. It seemed like the news cycle had stabilized a bit when I started writing this, but then there was news about another major crypto security incident at Binance . The crypto industry has a very long history of hacks , so it’s not the best industry to indicate vulnerabilities translating into new societal harm. Still, we are very much still living through the implications of this. The best guess for what is happening in the cybersecurity space is that the behind the scenes work has only accelerated, bringing more people and resources in to try and patch the internet — the Wall Street Journal reported that cyber first responders are strained , which seems like the system working. We’re living through this plot of an exponential rise in vulnerabilities, which will take a long time to level off at the top of the sigmoid. A few weeks ago, before the rapid acceleration in vulnerability disclosures and the uptick in reported hacks, I wrote the following take. It’s been getting a pretty consistent barrage of feedback, some hopeless dunk attempts and some reasonable discussion, so I wanted to unpack where I stand. When Claude Mythos was announced, it was previewed as if it was a new class of cyber weapon, where if it ended up in the wrong hands it would’ve caused mass societal destabilization. By all measures, GLM-5.3 is the model that crosses that threshold of capability, and there’s little public evidence that much has changed, and we’re over a month out of the model weight release. In fact, I would go further. If Claude Mythos was accidentally released as open-weight, it seems like the world would have been more or less fine. Yes, there would be a clear increase in cybersecurity incidents and it would be bad for society if the model leaked, but it would be a scenario that looks more like an acceleration than a step change in risk. The leading proponents of this new wave of open-weight fear mongering have effectively been making a falsifiable prediction — that the current open-weight models are going to cause substantial, not seen before AI harms by crippling our cyber infrastructure. Based on all the evidence I have, which I’ve unpacked above, they’re set up to be wrong. At least now, after so many years of debating open weight risks, we will start to get some real answers. To start the reflection, I wanted to do more due diligence and track down some receipts on the claim that the AI safety community was reacting as if open-weight Mythos would be an actual disaster, and not just a painful headache. This was distinctly my impression having lived through the online discourse. I’ve gotten criticism that the frontier AI community never said it would be a “true disaster,” but regardless of exactly what they said, it is always about how people hear and internalize your information. Here are some examples of the sort of language that I felt was too exaggerated and from prominent people, which spilled into the public and more importantly federal government perspective that this was a cyber weapon include: Rob Wiblin, host of the 80,000 hours podcast, on his own podcast (April 10, 2026): “If it fell into the hands of criminals or hostile state cyber actors, it would be an actual disaster.” Anthropic, in the Project Glasswing announcement blog (April 7, 2026): “Given the rate of AI progress, it will not be long before such capabilities proliferate, potentially beyond actors who are committed to deploying them safely. The fallout—for economies, public safety, and national security—could be severe.” For one that is actually more reasonable, to illustrate the fine lines between correct and exaggerated, from Zvi Mowshowitz (who I don’t agree with a ton of things on) on April 9, 2026: “Claude Mythos would give attackers a cornucopia of zero-day exploits for essentially all the software on Earth … It would be chaos.” To date, this chaos has been confined to those running large-scale digital products, which is good, but could change. I largely still stand by my above writing a few weeks ago, but I’m nervous about it. I’m not a cyber expert, I’m working hard to make the most educated predictions I can. It’s a fine line between “all of our tech companies need to work extra hard to keep us secure” and “public infrastructure is actually going down.” It is very clear as of writing this that there are way more critical vulnerabilities which are being found in popular tools and fixes are being built. For example, Epoch AI recently published a nice post on their internal work using GLM-5.3 to try and find vulnerabilities and chain them into what could be an attack. The actual exploit they found in Firefox is a good example of why cyber risks need multiple things to align for harm to be done: We used GLM 5.3 to create a website that, simply when visited by a Firefox user and without further interaction, gave the attacker the ability to exfiltrate files from the user’s computer. Here, the exploit is in Firefox, and a would-be hacker needs to plant a website that is looking for this exploit. This is doable, and could have serious consequences, but just finding the exploit is only one step in a multi-stage process. In the previous post, I should’ve been more specific on what “fine” is for a future of cybersecurity, and in this case it means giving more credit to some of the AI safety community that discussed this reasonably as a new era in cyber instability. Reflecting on it, I’m not sure fine is the right word to describe what is inevitably coming – a forced industry update to a new way of working with software, which will clearly be expensive and accompanied by some hard work. If you’re already somber about the challenges coming from AI, I think fine is actually very suitable. If you didn’t price in a period of turbulence, fine undersells. I’ve written many times that I am in the former, difficulty will come, group — but I think humans are good at muddling through problems and patching immediate concerns. What my view was closer to is that open models are providing balance in the offense-defense equation, and that Mythos coming sooner wouldn’t have massively upended this. I suspect most of these companies would be faster to adopt open-weight models than attackers, as most attackers are lower resourced than these companies. A key needle we’re watching the balance on is how willing attackers are to cause physical harm within the U.S. its allies. For now, while our adversaries have likely used these models and exploits to extract information en-masse in a clandestine way, it is not clear if there is a party who will cause mass harm by pushing the full force of these models at public institutions. I thought this Tweet was a funny way to summarize some of the personnel / motive gaps in hacking: Life is a lot easier once you stop seeing threat actors as hackers who want to break into systems by any means possible, and start seeing them as businesses with well defined business processes. A bakery isn’t going to start making dog food because there’s a dog food shortage. ClickFix and Phishing actors aren’t going to drop everything to vibecode exploits just because a critical CVE came out. The fact that the only actors exploiting this are the actors whose MO is exploiting things... isn’t a coincidence. It’s entirely predictable if you understand threat actor behavior. Where I sit, I expect most of these vulnerabilities are being found by closed models, but I have very high error bars on this prediction. A lot hinges on how open models are actually being used in the near term.

item.title: nemotron-halloween
item.abstract:
Back to Articles nemotron-halloween Enterprise + Article Published October 30, 2026 Upvote 3 Rick Grandy rgrandy Follow nvidia Maryam Motamedi maryameee Follow nvidia Building a Haunted House with NVIDIA Nemotron Open Models Or rather… Boo! Now Get Off My Lawn! TL;DR: MonsterHouse is an interactive projection I created for Halloween. He listens to trick-or-treaters, answers in the voice of a grumpy old pirate ship and softens when visitors remember their manners. He is built on the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent with NVIDIA Nemotron ASR , Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB , Magpie TTS Zeroshot and Audio2Face-3D , and he runs on a single workstation. I wanted the kids visiting my house at Halloween to interact in a fun and unique way. The house was going to be in charge and giving out the treats, but more grumpy than scary. Somehow, my solution was to give the garage door a mouth and teach him to complain. That became MonsterHouse: a grumpy old building with pirate stories, a fiery grin and a suspicious weakness for “please.” NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent supplies the conversation foundation. Nemotron Speech does the listening, Bolt E4B is the brain, NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot is the live voice, and NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D makes the wooden mouth talk. How Monster House works Listening: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 ASR turns visitor speech into text. [CONFIRMED: nemotron-speech-streaming-en-0.6b.q8_0.gguf ] Thinking: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB , an open small language model for conversational agents, writes each reply. A LoRA adapter supplies the personality. Speaking: NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot voices each reply from a short reference sample of the character. Animating: NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D turns clean speech into mouth animation in Unreal Engine 5. Seeing: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni describes costumes, while YOLO and ByteTrack count and track visitors. Running it: NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent coordinates everything on one workstation with an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q and an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell. A grin full of splinters The mouth came first. I imagined the wooden garage door boards splitting into jagged lips, with the burning flames of hell illuminating the driveway from beyond whenever he opened his cursed mouth. He needed to look ancient, expressive and mildly offended by the existence of visitors. A few expressions from a house with plenty to say. Creating a custom animation rig was one of the more labor intensive parts of the build. After bashing it into submission, I could export the facial expression shapes that Audio2Face-3D could later animate. The character SkelMesh was built in Autodesk Maya then exported into Unreal Engine where virtual fire and effects were added behind the door. With no eyes, no eyebrows and no blinking, he’s a surprisingly economical monster. While all the nonsense of building the character was going on, NVIDIA built the Nemotron Voice Agent. What was supposed to be the hard part of the build now became rather fun, iterative and easy. I had a foundation for listening, conversation and speech right out of the box. The house already had a mouth. Now he could finally find something to complain about. Teaching bad manners The house needed a past as cantankerous as its personality so I devised a backstory that the house had been built from the timbers of a sunken pirate ship, haunted by its stormy past. The nautical complaints now had a reason. This was the ship, reincarnated as real estate and not entirely pleased about it. The performance needed a guide, a path to follow from greeting to goodbye while providing treats along the way. First, the house would brush visitors off with remarks like “I’m busy grumbling, go bother the neighbors!” But persistence would wear him down. A “Please” could break through immediately, and “thank you” earned a warm farewell. Once a visitor won him over, I wanted him to stay won over. Nobody wants to negotiate with the same garage door twice. Here is where the Voice Agent really shines. You can choose any LLM you like. Because I wanted the system to be off-grid and completely self-contained, I had a memory and compute budget. The character needs more than a prompt that says “be grumpy.” It had to follow a master conversation flow, respond to what visitors actually said, track encounter state, and leave enough compute for the rest of the pipeline. After testing more than a dozen models, I landed on Bolt E4B to supply the live dialogue. It is an open small language model purpose-built for local conversational agents and interactive characters, which is a fair description of a talking garage door. I use the 4-bit quantized release (the “4GB” in its name) as the default response model, with the BF16 checkpoint available for comparison. If it’s not obvious by now, I work at NVIDIA and due to this I was able to test Bolt E4B before its public release and found it to be a solid choice, with a smaller footprint than other frontrunners- Qwen3 30B-A3B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B. It works inside the Nemotron Voice Agent pipeline, turning what visitors say into the next suitably reluctant reply. Bolt provides the conversational foundation. My prompts, application logic and LoRA adapter trained on thousands of reviewed example conversations shape it into this particular stubborn ship. Creating a dataset of over 5000 multi-turn conversations meant I could train LoRAs for each model I felt good enough to be an option. Some took about an hour to train, some took a couple. A local agent ran everything and benchmarked the results. That agent and a very large LLM created and judged the dataset to begin with. This happened at night or while I was doing the day job. With the LoRA in place I check the replies for continuity, timing and tone, benchmark models and adapters for quality, repetition and speed, and then listen to the performance. The house should give in eventually, without turning into a cheerful concierge. A little resistance is part of the charm. An endless argument with a garage door is not. A voice worth waiting for Two shortcuts, two outputs. Authored text skips fresh dialogue generation, and saved audio skips synthesis. Clean speech drives the animation separately from the audience effects. A haunted house loses authority if he takes too long to complain. The pipeline releases speakable text before an entire answer is finished, so the house can start talking while the rest of the sentence is still on its way. Prepared greetings and candy jokes cover familiar encounters: the text bank saves language-model work, and cached recordings save speech synthesis. Even an ancient grump benefits from rehearsing. median end-of-speech-to-audio with Bolt Q4 & TTS = 1.70 seconds
median end-of-speech-to-audio cached responses = 0.72 seconds
(note: speech-end detection currently waits for 300 ms of silence ) NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot turns text into the Queen’s English. Its zero-shot voice conditioning uses a short reference sample instead of a trained voice; mine supplies the grumpy pirate character. The house has seven moods, from grumpy and menacing to amused and delighted, and emotion tags dictated by the prompt template and provided by the LLM choose how each line is delivered. Since each emotion requires a different 3-10 second voice sample I added a “Sample your Voice” block on the UI’s tool tab. I could then read and record a sample line of text in my best happy pirate or angry pirate voice. When it’s “Go” time, Bolt E4B decides what to say, and Magpie turns that text into speech with the proper delight or despair. Next down the pipe is Audio2Face-3D and the 3d character scene I created in Epic’s Unreal Engine. The default model weights work best with a clean neutral male or female voice, not too deep, not too high (choose the appropriate gendered model for your use case). I wanted the house to have a very deep and demonic voice with echo and chamber.

item.title: Run AI Models for Edge Application Development with Just a Few Commands
item.abstract:
AI is expanding beyond the data center as developers build a new generation of agents to act at the edge: monitoring driver attention and cabin conditions, helping robots understand their surroundings and plan tasks, and coordinating fleets of machines on production lines. These physical AI applications rely on models that perceive, reason, and act within tight memory, power, and latency budgets. But getting a model ready to run can involve substantial setup. NVIDIA DGX Spark, now available in a 64GB configuration , gives embedded developers a platform to prototype, fine-tune, and test models and agents. NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM provides a lightweight C++ inference runtime designed for embedded workloads, bringing the same inference framework to development on Spark and deployment on platforms such as NVIDIA Jetson Thor , NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor , and NVIDIA IGX Thor . You can get started in just a few commands with the trtedge command-line interface (CLI). It downloads your selected model and builds TensorRT engines optimized for inference on Spark. In this tutorial, you’ll run NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning , a text-only model, on Spark using TensorRT Edge-LLM. You’ll test prompts in your terminal and serve the model through an API for application prototyping. You’ll also enable DSpark speculative decoding to accelerate generation. Prerequisites: Set up your development environment To get started, you’ll need a DGX Spark with a supported NVIDIA software stack, NVIDIA CUDA 13, TensorRT 10.16.1.11 or newer within the 10.x series, and Python 3.10 to 3.12. The examples below were tested with TensorRT Edge-LLM 0.11.1 and TensorRT 10.16.1.11. Open a terminal on your DGX Spark, create and activate a virtual environment, and install TensorRT Edge-LLM: python3 -m venv --system-site-packages .venv-edgellm
source .venv-edgellm/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install "tensorrt-edgellm[server]==0.11.1" Note: The virtual environment keeps newly installed packages separate while allowing access to all system Python packages, including TensorRT. Check the TensorRT version and confirm that the TensorRT Edge-LLM runtime loads: python -c "import tensorrt as trt; v = tuple(map(int, trt.__version__.split('.'))); assert (10, 16, 1, 11) <= v < (11,), f'TensorRT >=10.16.1.11 and <11 required; found {trt.__version__}'; from tensorrt_edgellm import runtime; runtime.load()" Note: If compatible system TensorRT bindings are unavailable, follow the NVIDIA TensorRT pip installation instructions to install a compatible TensorRT 10.x version in the activated environment, then rerun the verification command. With the virtual environment still active, start a chat with Nemotron-3.5 Lightning: trtedge chat nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 On your first launch, wait for the model download (approximately 21GB) and engine build to finish. Files are stored in ~/.cache/tensorrt-edgellm by default, so allow space for both the model and engines. Later launches reuse matching cached engines. Once the chat prompt appears, enter: Convert 25°C to Fahrenheit. Answer in one sentence. Example response: 25°C is equal to 77°F. Continue the conversation with follow-up questions, or type /exit to end the session. Serve your model Serve your model through a local OpenAI-compatible API on Spark for application development and testing. With your virtual environment active, start the server: trtedge serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8000 The server builds or reuses an engine for this configuration. Once startup completes, open a second terminal on your DGX Spark and check that it is ready: curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8000/health/ready A response containing "status":"ready" confirms that the server is ready. Send your first prompt to the chat completions endpoint: curl -fsS -N http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4", "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "Convert 25°C to Fahrenheit. Answer in one sentence." } ], "stream": true, "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 128
}' The response streams as JSON events. Keep the server running for more requests, or press Ctrl+C in the server terminal to stop it. Optional: Enable speculative decoding You can speed up generation with DSpark speculative decoding , which uses a draft model to propose several tokens for the main model to verify in a single pass. To enable it with three draft tokens, press Ctrl+C in the server terminal, then restart the server with DSpark enabled: trtedge serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8000 \ --speculative-config '{ "method": "dspark", "model": "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4-DSpark", "num_speculative_tokens": 3 }' Once the server is ready, send another prompt to the chat completions endpoint to try DSpark-enabled generation. You can experiment with num_speculative_tokens and other settings to tune generation speed for your workload. See the speculative decoding documentation to learn more . Performance on DGX Spark 64GB TensorRT Edge-LLM delivers low response latency and fast token generation with NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning on DGX Spark 64GB. The table below reports time to first token (TTFT) and generation speed with and without DSpark speculative decoding. Decoding Workload Median TTFT (ms) Mean generation speed (tokens/s) DSpark OFF SpeedBench 1K 201.0 73.3 DSpark OFF SpeedBench 2K 329.5 72.8 DSpark OFF HumanEval prompts 98.1 73.4 DSpark ON SpeedBench 1K 203.0 108.5 DSpark ON SpeedBench 2K 331.6 105.3 DSpark ON HumanEval prompts 98.7 126.9 Table 1. Nemotron-3.5 Lightning performance on DGX Spark 64GB with and without DSpark speculative decoding. Generation speed is the average token generation rate per request, excluding time to first token. DSpark uses three draft tokens. Peak total system memory use during inference with DSpark was 27.9GB, including the OS. Measured on DGX Spark 64GB running DGX OS 7.6.0 (Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS), using NVFP4 with thinking enabled, batch size one, one concurrent streaming request, and a 128-token output limit. Average input lengths were 1,153 tokens for SpeedBench 1K, 2,247 for SpeedBench 2K, and 139 for HumanEval. Next steps Try another model from the supported models list and continue developing your application on Spark. Options include vision-language models that interpret images and video, as well as speech recognition and text-to-speech models. Explore the TensorRT Edge-LLM documentation for model-specific workflows and requirements on your target embedded platform. And visit the Nemotron developer page for resources to get started.
