item.title: Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry
item.abstract: Google Suncatcher’s prototype space data center is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications. After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus: Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨ Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite. A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally. The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor. Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools. Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation. If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links. Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively. Companies like Starcloud and Cowboy Space expect to perform inference loads on individual satellites. Google and SpaceX’s visions are closely linked. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, holds a significant investment stake in SpaceX. And to launch their orbital data centers, both companies will require Starship, the still-in-development heavy-lift rocket at the center of Elon Musk’s space vision, to be fully and rapidly reusable. In a peer-reviewed analysis published earlier this month, Suncatcher researchers estimated that SpaceX would need to fly Starship 1,800 times to achieve the same learning-driven cost reductions it saw with its earlier vehicles. Suncatcher is a classic Google moonshot — the company’s focus is on designing infrastructure that will be economical in the 2030s. Getting there, however, may depend on how the rest of the company responds to the pressures and opportunities of AI in the near term. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, saw its stock plunge this week after reporting that efforts to insert AI into its search businesses are hurting ad revenue growth. Correction: The Suncatcher prototype satellite has four TPUs onboard, but can only operate one at a time.

item.abstract:
Herdr Herdr is a desktop app for terminals and coding agents. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window. Install Linux and macOS curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can build from source . Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64. The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in ~/.local/bin .
Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks.
On macOS the app lives in ~/Applications/Herdr.app .
For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download Herdr.dmg and drag Herdr to Applications. Windows Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer): irm https: // releases.herdr.dev / app / install.ps1 | iex Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up. Both installers download and run code. Read the shell installer or PowerShell installer first if you prefer.
They also install herdr-core if it is missing.
The app can help install or update a core it cannot use. Find your work A space holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has tabs . Split a tab into panes to put terminals or mod panels beside each other. An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays.
New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder. The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent.
Agents that report status show as: Working: still busy. Blocked: waiting for you. Done: finished while you were looking elsewhere. Idle: not working, or a finished agent you have looked at. Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in peek , over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work.
Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS.
An address such as t7 means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. vps/t7 names one on another machine. The window arranges terminals. The core runs them.
Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals.
After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs. Work on another machine Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action.
Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it.
Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer. Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom.
Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up. Make it yours Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences.
The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98.
A layout arranges the window. Mods are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs. Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start.
Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it.
A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error. Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in keys.json ; see the keys section of the mod guide for the format. Layouts and mods · Commands Updates and privacy Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core.
Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette.
Builds from source do not update themselves. Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy.
Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read security and privacy before installing someone else's mod. For agents herdr-app --skill This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-core skill points agents here.
Use herdr-core for running and coordinating programs; use the app to change what you see. herdr-app ls
herdr-app status
herdr-app commands The first two inspect the open window. The command list also works without one.
See the command reference for arguments. Build from source For bugs, mod API requests and code contributions, see Contributing . Clone this repo with its submodules. Use Rust 1.95.0 and Zig 0.16.0, the versions used in CI .
Linux needs the development packages listed in that workflow. git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app.git cd herdr-app
just build
just test just install Install just to use these recipes.
The platform installer builds a release and adds the app to your desktop.
On Linux it links to this checkout, so keep the checkout in place.
Quit and reopen Herdr to use the new build. Documentation checks also need Bun : just docs-check checks generated pages and CLI examples; just docs-generate refreshes the reference pages. To compare drawing changes on Windows, Linux or macOS, run the same fixed workloads against each build: python scripts/bench.py --bin < app executable > --set spinners --seconds 20 The runner requires hc on PATH and uses the Python executable running the script. It prints a unique artifact folder with the run settings, counters and results, then stops its private app, terminals and core. Both sets use Python fixture programs; the default set’s TUI workload replaces historical btop measurements. --only spinners measures just the quiet native spinner scenario. Keep the window visible and the display awake, and compare the same window activity and display settings; inactive windows may draw at a lower rate. Windows records visibility, foreground activity and display Hz at each measurement boundary; other platforms mark these observations unavailable. Visibility does not establish occlusion. Draws are window render calls. Render-to-paint elapsed time stops before scene finalization, backend drawing, uploads and presentation; it is separate from OS process CPU time. Neither measures physical presentation or the FPS HUD’s derived MAX FPS. python scripts/bench_compare.py ghostty --root <artifact folder> reuses a run’s fake agent for the macOS comparison. Benchmark checks: python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_bench.py .

item.title: Vibe Coding a Classic Game: Building Breakout Step by Step with an AI Assistant
item.abstract:
Vibe Coding a Classic Game: Building Breakout Step by Step with an AI Assistant Vibe coding is a workflow where you describe what you want in natural language and let an AI agent handle code generation, execution, and iteration rather than typing every line yourself. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on October 30, 2026 in Programming Vibe coding is a genuinely new way of building software, not a rebrand of an old one, and it deserves a real definition before this tutorial uses it a hundred more times. The term was coined by Andrej Karpathy in early 2025 to describe a workflow where you describe what you want in natural language and let an AI agent handle code generation, execution, and iteration rather than typing every line yourself. It caught on fast enough that Collins English Dictionary named it their Word of the Year for 2025 , and by 2026 it's not a novelty; it's a standard way real software gets built. This article is a genuine, start-to-finish vibe coding project: building the classic arcade game Breakout , using an AI coding assistant to generate every piece, with every prompt shown, every resulting code block explained in real detail, and the complete, tested game assembled at the end. This isn't a toy example. Every line of code in this article was actually written and verified before publication; the collision physics, the win and loss conditions, all of it, ran through real automated tests rather than being assumed to work. What Is Vibe Coding? The mechanical description is simple: you describe a goal, an AI agent generates code toward it, you review and iterate, and you repeat until it does what you need. What's changed since the term appeared is the sophistication of the agents doing the generating; current tools don't just autocomplete a line, they can read an entire project, edit multiple files, run the code, and fix what breaks, all from a natural-language instruction. Airbnb, for example, reports that AI now writes around 60% of its new code . The current tool landscape is worth knowing before picking one: Claude Code is a terminal-native agent well suited to exactly this kind of project: describe a feature, and watch it write and test the code directly in your project folder Cursor is an AI-native code editor for people who want that same power inside a familiar IDE Replit Agent is built with beginners specifically in mind, and it walks through a visible plan before writing code, which is genuinely useful for understanding the "why" behind each step, not just the "what" Bolt.new and v0 are faster paths to a working prototype for people who don't want to touch a terminal at all The Game We're Building: Breakout Breakout is one of the most influential arcade games ever made, and its backstory matters because it explains why the game is structured the way it is. Atari released Breakout on May 13, 1976 , conceptualized by Nolan Bushnell and Steve Bristow as a single-player evolution of Pong, and built by a young engineer named Steve Wozniak, working alongside his friend Steve Jobs. Wozniak's design was so aggressively minimized in its chip count that Atari's own manufacturing line reportedly couldn't replicate it and had to ship a version with more components instead. The two Steves would go on to found Apple together that same year, and Breakout's hardware logic directly influenced parts of the original Apple II's design. The rules are simple enough, which is exactly why it's a good vibe coding project: complex enough to need real logic, simple enough to fully understand end to end. A wall of bricks lines the top of the screen. A ball bounces around the play area, and you control a paddle at the bottom, moving it left and right to keep the ball in play. Every time the ball hits a brick, the brick is destroyed and you score points. If the ball gets past your paddle and falls off the bottom of the screen, you lose a life. Destroy every brick, and you win; run out of lives, and the game ends. Prerequisites You need less than you'd think: a modern web browser (Chrome, Firefox, or Safari all work fine), a text editor, and one AI coding assistant. This tutorial has zero build tools, zero frameworks, and zero dependencies to install; the entire game is one HTML file that runs by opening it in a browser. Setting up Claude Code: install it with npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code , then run claude from inside an empty project folder to start a session. If you'd rather use Cursor, Replit, or another tool from the list above, every prompt below works identically; just paste it into whichever assistant you've chosen. Here's the actual build, broken into the same stages you'd naturally prompt an AI assistant through, one real capability at a time rather than asking for the whole game in one shot, which tends to produce something harder to debug when it doesn't quite work. You can find the full code in this repo . Step 1: The Canvas and Game Skeleton Prompt : "Create a single HTML file for a Breakout game. Set up an HTML5 canvas 480 pixels wide and 400 pixels tall, centered on the page, with a dark background. Add a heading, and placeholder text elements for score and lives above the canvas. Don't add any game logic yet, just the skeleton."
Score: 0 Lives: 3
What this does: the canvas element is where every visual frame of the game gets drawn; it's a blank rectangle you control at the pixel level through JavaScript. Starting with just the skeleton, no logic, is deliberate: it lets you confirm the page structure actually renders correctly before adding anything that could break. That matters more with AI-generated code than hand-written code, since it's easier to spot exactly where something went wrong when you're only checking one small piece at a time. Step 2: The Paddle Prompt : "Add a paddle: an 80x10 pixel rectangle near the bottom of the canvas. Make it move left and right with the arrow keys, and keep it from moving off either edge of the canvas." const paddle = { width: 80, height: 10, x: (canvas.width - 80) / 2, y: canvas.height - 20, speed: 7, dx: 0 }; const keys = { left: false, right: false }; document.addEventListener("keydown", (e) => { if (e.key === "ArrowLeft") keys.left = true; if (e.key === "ArrowRight") keys.right = true; }); document.addEventListener("keyup", (e) => { if (e.key === "ArrowLeft") keys.left = false; if (e.key === "ArrowRight") keys.right = false; }); function updatePaddle() { if (keys.left) paddle.dx = -paddle.speed; else if (keys.right) paddle.dx = paddle.speed; else paddle.dx = 0; paddle.x += paddle.dx; paddle.x = Math.max(0, Math.min(canvas.width - paddle.width, paddle.x)); } What this does : keydown and keyup listeners track which arrow keys are currently held, rather than reacting once per press, which is what makes the paddle move smoothly while a key is held down instead of jumping once per keystroke. The last line of updatePaddle is the boundary check; Math.max and Math.min together clamp the paddle's position so it can never move past either edge of the canvas, a one-line fix for a bug that's easy to forget entirely until you watch the paddle vanish off-screen. Step 3: The Ball and Its Physics Prompt : "Add a ball: a small circle that starts near the bottom center of the canvas and moves diagonally. Make it bounce off the left, right, and top walls." const ball = { x: canvas.width / 2, y: canvas.height - 30, radius: 6, speed: 4, dx: 3, dy: -3 }; function updateBall() { ball.x += ball.dx; ball.y += ball.dy; if (ball.x + ball.radius > canvas.width || ball.x - ball.radius < 0) ball.dx *= -1; if (ball.y - ball.radius < 0) ball.dy *= -1; } What this does : dx and dy are the ball's velocity, how far it moves on each axis every frame, and updating position by simply adding them each frame is the entire basis of the game's motion.

item.title: The AI Skills That Actually Show Up in Job Postings Right Now
item.abstract: The AI Skills That Actually Show Up in Job Postings Right Now Which AI skills appear most often in job postings right now, and what do they mean for your career? By Vinod Chugani on October 29, 2026 in Career Advice Spend any time on a job board right now and you'll see AI mentioned everywhere. But there's a gap between what shows up as a vague requirement and what employers are actually screening for, and that gap matters if you're trying to build marketable skills rather than just adding buzzwords to your resume. This article draws on data from several large-scale analyses of job postings in 2025 and 2026 to show which AI skills appear most consistently, how demand breaks down by role type, and what that means for where you should focus your time. Why the Numbers Are Moving So Fast Here's the number to start with: an analysis of more than 360,000 job postings collected between late 2025 and mid-2026 found that AI is now the second most requested skill across all roles, appearing in roughly one in five postings. It ranked behind only communication, and ahead of Python, SQL, and cloud platforms like AWS. That alone would be notable. What makes the pattern more striking is the rate of change. Dice analyzed seven million U.S. tech job postings and found that AI skill requirements jumped from 15% of postings in January 2024 to 75% by mid-2026. Lightcast data cited by the Bipartisan Policy Center found that postings explicitly requiring AI-related skills increased 144% year over year. In data and analytics roles specifically, AI appears in close to 45% of postings. The takeaway: AI fluency is moving from a differentiator to a baseline expectation, and it's moving faster than most people's skill-building timelines. The Skills Employers Are Naming, by Category Not all AI skills carry equal weight, and demand isn't uniform across role types. Looking at the data, four broad categories emerge. AI Literacy and Prompt Engineering AI literacy is the most widely requested category and covers the broadest population of workers. It means a general understanding of what AI tools can and cannot do, how to use them effectively at work, and how to evaluate their outputs critically rather than just accepting them. Prompt engineering sits within this category and has seen dramatic growth. Dice found it among the fastest-growing AI skills by year-over-year demand, at 253% growth. LinkedIn 's 2026 labor market report showed that U.S. jobs requiring AI literacy skills, including prompt engineering, grew 70% year over year. Across the broader job posting dataset, prompt engineering shows up in 7% of all postings, ChatGPT proficiency in 6%, and large language model familiarity in 4%. One caveat: employers aren't hiring standalone prompt engineers. The skill appears most often as one component within a broader role — the same way Excel proficiency or internet research became baseline expectations rather than job titles. The most valuable position in most fields is what some workforce analysts call "prompting plus something," where the AI skill amplifies domain expertise rather than replacing it. Agentic AI and Workflow Automation This is the fastest-growing category by rate of change, though it's still concentrated in technical roles. Stanford's 2026 AI Index found that the share of AI job postings mentioning agentic AI rose from 0.69% to 18.9% in a single year. Dice's analysis of seven million postings shows that demand for agentic AI grew 587% year over year, with AI agents themselves growing 503%. What this looks like in practice: employers are increasingly looking for people who understand how AI systems can be configured to take sequences of actions autonomously, often using tools like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), vector databases, and agent orchestration frameworks. A 2026 analysis of 390 AI engineer postings found that 56% mentioned AI evaluation, 50% mentioned AI agents, and 26% required experience with RAG specifically. For non-technical professionals, the relevant takeaway isn't that you need to build these systems. It's that familiarity with what agentic workflows are and what they can accomplish has become expected in roles that work alongside engineering teams. Machine Learning Foundations Machine learning remains the most consistently requested foundational technical skill across the full history of AI hiring, even as newer categories grow faster from a smaller base. Roles requiring machine learning knowledge are concentrated in engineering, data science, and research, but the terminology appears far more broadly. What's shifted in 2026 is the specificity of requests. Earlier postings often listed machine learning as a general requirement. Current postings more frequently ask for experience with particular parts of the machine learning lifecycle: model evaluation, fine-tuning, and machine learning operations (MLOps) — the infrastructure and processes needed to move machine learning systems from experimentation into production. Data engineering, which involves building the pipelines and storage systems that feed machine learning models, currently tops recruiter search data from platforms like SignalHire , ahead of both AI engineering and data science roles. This demand reflects a practical constraint: companies that have invested in AI capabilities often hit bottlenecks at the data layer before they ever get to the modeling layer. AI Governance, Ethics, and Responsible AI This category sits in a complicated place in the data. On one hand, it appears in LinkedIn's 2026 Skills on the Rise report as a top priority for business-side hiring. Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index found that nearly half of corporate interactions with AI assistants are now focused on cognitive work like analysis, evaluation, and strategic thinking, which raises the stakes around governance frameworks for those outputs. On the other hand, actual job posting data tells a quieter story: AI governance and responsible AI terms each appear in only around 1.5% of postings, and employer adoption has been slower than you might expect given how broadly AI is now deployed. The World Economic Forum estimates that 22% of current jobs will shift structurally by 2030, which raises compliance and ethics questions that most organizations haven't yet built systematic hiring pipelines to address. Practically speaking, governance skills are unlikely to be why someone gets hired initially, but they're increasingly what separates candidates at senior and principal-level roles. Qarera 's analysis found that AI skill requirements appear in 39.5% of principal-level postings, roughly double the overall average. How Demand Differs Across Functions One of the more important shifts in the 2026 data is where AI skill requirements are showing up outside of technical roles. Lightcast found that 51% of job postings requiring AI skills sit outside IT and computer science, across sectors including healthcare, finance, marketing, and human resources. In product management roles specifically, AI appeared as a required skill in 37% of postings in Qarera's dataset. For design roles, the figure was 23.1%, and for business analyst roles, 19.1%. These aren't engineering roles, and the AI skills being requested aren't engineering skills. They reflect an expectation that professionals in these functions can work effectively alongside AI systems, make sense of their outputs, and judge when and where to apply them. LinkedIn's 2026 report captured this direction clearly: employers are looking for professionals who can define AI value propositions, not only build systems. That framing matters for how non-technical professionals think about positioning their skills. What the Pay Data Suggests Salary data is an imperfect signal, but the direction in the current market is consistent. Postings that mention AI skills pay roughly 28% more than equivalent roles that don't, according to analysis from multiple hiring platforms.

item.title: How to Check and Configure NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage for Your Platform
item.abstract: NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage (GDS) accelerates GPU storage access in on-premises and cloud environments. It provides a robust, portable, and efficient data path between NVIDIA GPUs and storage targets to increase bandwidth, minimize latency, and reduce CPU and memory utilization across a broad range of platforms, application frameworks, and workload patterns . Configuring NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage starts with understanding your environment. Which settings and storage paths are appropriate for your platform and workload? Extensive documentation describes how to configure and troubleshoot supported architectures and storage solutions, but you must navigate this information and optimize your deployment. Figure 1. High-level diagram of the GPUDirect Storage data path with gds-diag The gds-diag tool was developed by the GPUDirect Storage team to simplify optimization and configuration of GPUDirect Storage. gds-diag is a simple, open-source command-line utility that assesses environments, identifies problems, and suggests improvements to help you make the most of your GDS deployment. It is also bundled with an optional agent skill that adds a natural-language interface and orchestration layer. The skill interprets your intent, selects and invokes the appropriate subcommands, and coordinates multi-step diagnostic workflows. Beyond command selection and routing, the skill extends gds-diag with model-guided reasoning. It can interpret diagnostic results, apply relevant system context, and propose or carry out appropriate remediation. This post shows you how to get started with gds-diag using either the command-line interface or the agent skill. Download and installation To use gds-diag , you need a Linux system with Python 3.8 or newer. GPUDirect Storage requires an NVIDIA datacenter-class GPU and NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit 12.2 or newer, but these are not dependencies of gds-diag itself. gds-diag is distributed as part of the NVIDIA Magnum IO GitHub repository with no other dependencies to install. Clone the repository on the machine where you plan to run it with git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/MagnumIO.git and select one of the following usage models: Command-line tool: This provides a deterministic, minimal-dependency path to diagnose GDS deployments. Go to the gds-diag directory, run gds-diag.py --help , and follow the Command-line usage guidance. AI agent: This provides the most intuitive, flexible, interactive, natural-language mechanism to diagnose GDS deployments while still retaining the reliable determinism of the underlying command-line tool. Open the gds-diag directory in your preferred AI coding assistant and follow the Agent skill usage guidance. Quick tip: The AI agent mode is recommended if this option is available in your environment. gds-diag is validated with both Claude and Codex, though it may work with other tools as well. Command-line usage The gds-diag command-line tool is a single Python script with multiple subcommands to focus on different diagnostic tasks. You can browse available subcommands by running ./gds-diag.py --help . For more information about a specific subcommand, run ./gds-diag.py <subcommand> --help . Quick tip: Not sure where to start? Just run ./gds-diag.py all /path/to/check , and gds-diag will automatically run a complete sequence of diagnostics for that path. This works in bare-metal, virtual machine, and container environments. Figure 2 groups the available subcommands into four categories. Figure 2. Table of gds-diag subcommands, grouped into categories Choose a diagnostic category based on your stage of deployment or the problem you need to investigate. End-to-end checks: Use all to automatically select appropriate diagnostics for your environment and run them in sequence. Preparing for installation: Use pre-install to check GPU support and CUDA Toolkit installation. Use support-matrix to view supported storage targets and plan your deployment. Validating an installation: Use post-install to check whether GDS is installed correctly and identify blockers. Use config-audit to review configuration files and environment variables that influence GDS behavior. Deep diagnostics: Use container-check to assess GDS support in container environments, including containerd, Docker, Enroot, and Kubernetes. Use mount-check to diagnose a specific mount point or directory. The anatomy of a gds-diag finding The output of most gds-diag subcommands is presented as a set of findings grouped into sections, as Figure 3 shows. Figure 3. Screenshot of an example gds-diag finding with annotations Each finding and each section has a status badge. “FAIL” indicates a hard blocker. “WARN” indicates a potential blocker. “INFO” communicates notable information. “PASS” indicates a nominal finding and is shown only when you use the --verbose option. Each finding includes an explanation followed by a mitigation plan. gds-diag will not implement the mitigation plan or otherwise modify the system on its own . Its role is to identify problems and optimization opportunities and help you or your administrator make improvements. Multiple sections (and findings within those sections) may be shown. Quick tip: You can also emit all diagnostic reports as structured JSON data with the --json command-line option. This could be useful if you plan to ingest findings into another tool or archive them for future reference. Most subcommands follow the same structure. The gds-diag.py support-matrix command is a notable exception: it emits output in the form of a table with footnotes. This subcommand shows which platform combinations GDS supports. Use the --static option to present general data (shown in Figure 4) or the --live option to incorporate information from the system as presently configured. Figure 4. Screenshot of gds-diag support matrix Items marked in green are fully supported, items marked in yellow are supported depending on architectural or configuration caveats, and items marked in red are not supported. Quick tip: Most distributed storage vendors elect to present their file systems as nfs or nfs4 at the Linux operating system level, so this row of the support matrix corresponds to a broad range of product support. Command-line demo To demonstrate, consider preparing a new or modified GDS configuration file for production deployment. The config-audit subcommand is an ideal choice for this scenario. If called with no arguments, it will audit the current effective configuration, including both static configuration files and dynamic environment variable modifiers. The following example uses the --config option to specify a candidate configuration to review. Figure 5. Command-line demonstration of gds-diag identifying a configuration file error The configuration audit reveals a misspelled entry in the configuration file. After you correct the error, config-audit confirms that the configuration is valid and provides additional informational hints. Agent skill usage The gds-diag agent skill activates automatically when you open the gds-diag repository using a coding assistant such as Claude or Codex. Quick tip: You can explicitly activate gds-diag using the /gds-diag keyword in your coding assistant, but this isn’t strictly necessary. It will automatically choose it as the appropriate skill to use if you ask natural language questions about GDS. The skill does not attempt to duplicate deterministic checks that are already provided by the gds-diag command-line tool. Instead, its primary role is to aid in routing between gds-diag subcommands and interpreting their output. The following are a few examples of queries you could pose using the skill: Is this system eligible to use GDS? Is it available for /mnt/data ? How do I configure GDS optimally to access /mnt/data ? What configuration files are being used by GDS? Do any configuration parameters need to be updated? Which NVMe device has the best locality to GPU3?
